Augustus. The first emperor of the Roman Empire, born Gaius Octavius and adopted heir of his great-uncle Julius Caesar. Emerging victorious from the civil wars that followed Caesar's assassination, Augustus ruled from 27 BC until his death in AD 14 and transformed Rome from a republic into an imperial power while initiating the Pax Romana, an era of relative peace and cultural flourishing.

He defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the naval Battle of Actium in 31 BC. Working together with Mark Antony and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, he formed the Second Triumvirate to defeat Caesar's assassins. An extensive building program gave him the chance to boast that he found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble. Yet his forces suffered a devastating defeat in the Teutoburg Forest, where three Roman legions under Varus were annihilated by Germanic tribes. He exiled the poet Ovid to the Black Sea, though the specific reason—described only as a poem and a mistake—remains unspecified. In 27 BC, the Roman Senate granted him the title Augustus, meaning "the revered one," marking the traditional start of the Roman Empire.

He was the stepfather of Tiberius, the reluctant successor Augustus eventually chose for the imperial throne. Julius Caesar was his great-uncle and adoptive father, whose assassination propelled him into politics. Mark Antony served as his primary political rival and former ally in the Second Triumvirate. Cleopatra, the Egyptian queen whom he defeated at Actium, was crucial to securing his sole control of the Roman world.
